checks.prompt: A team on this cloud provider needs three things: spoken prompts for their phone menus, narration of long articles, and word-level timings so a web player can highlight text as it is read. They also want to transcribe customer calls. Which of the four does this service cover, and what should they do about the rest?
checks.explanation: This service is synthesis only — the provider's recognition offering is a completely separate service. What it does cover well is the other three: an engine ladder that includes one tuned for paragraphs and articles, and a mode where you ask for timing metadata rather than audio, returning word, sentence, viseme and markup offsets that are the raw material for captions, karaoke-style highlighting and avatar lip-sync.
options: It covers the first three: managed synthesis with engines tuned for different content — including one aimed at long-form passages — and a mode that returns word, sentence, viseme and markup timing metadata instead of audio, which is exactly what caption highlighting and lip-sync are built from. Transcription is a different service from the same provider entirely; this one is synthesis only
It covers all four, since the same call transcribes audio when given an audio input rather than text
It covers only the phone prompts; long-form narration requires a self-hosted model because of request size limits, and timing metadata must be derived by aligning the audio afterwards
It covers the first three and also transcription, but transcription requires a separate credential and region

checks.prompt: Describe this service's request model and say why it is called stateless. Name the two axes that decide how any given call is made, and explain what happens at each end of the second axis. Then explain the character-counting rule that makes this service different from at least one competitor, and why two different limits exist.
checks.expected: A correct answer must establish the shape: every call is self-contained — text or markup in, audio bytes out — with no session and no model loaded on your side, so a request describes what to say, who says it, which quality engine, and what container. The first axis is quality and cost, selected by the engine: a cheap basic one, a natural neural one, and pricier tiers tuned for long passages and for the most expressive conversational delivery — with the constraint that a voice must actually support the engine chosen. The second axis is SIZE: short text is synthesised inline and the response is a streaming body read like a file, while long text goes through an asynchronous task that writes the result into object storage and returns a task identifier you poll until it reports completion. The character rule must be stated precisely: only the spoken text is billed and the markup tags are NOT — which is the opposite of at least one competing service that bills every character of markup. The two limits follow from that: the BILLED count decides the bill, while the TOTAL count, tags included, decides whether the request fits, so the synchronous path has both a total and a billed ceiling and the asynchronous path has much larger versions of both. The practical consequence is that a heavily marked-up document can sit far under the billed ceiling and still be too large to send inline. Noting that timing metadata is requested as an output format rather than as a separate call, or that custom pronunciations come from uploaded lexicons attached per request, is a plus.

checks.prompt: Three failures on one integration. A request using the most expressive engine with a voice that has always worked is rejected. A response is written to a file with a wave extension and nothing will play it. And a second attempt to read the returned audio yields nothing. What are the three causes?
checks.explanation: Three independent facts. Engines are a property of the voice — the newest and priciest ones are available on a subset only, so the catalogue lookup reporting each voice's supported engines is the thing to consult. Raw sample output is exactly that: signed samples with no container and no header, so it will not play until you wrap it or you ask for a self-describing format instead. And the audio in the response is a streaming body rather than a bytes object: read it once, and read it at all, or you leak the connection.
options: Engine support is per voice — the newest engines exist on a subset of voices, so the pairing must be checked from the voice catalogue rather than assumed. The unplayable file is raw sample output, which has no container or header at all, so it must be wrapped before anything will play it, or a self-describing format requested instead. And the returned audio is a stream that is consumed once: reading it a second time yields nothing
The rejected engine means the region does not bill for it yet; the unplayable file means the sample rate was not specified; and the empty second read means the response object expired after a timeout
All three are permission problems: the identity lacks rights to the newer engine, to write files, and to re-read the stream

The rejected engine means markup was used without declaring it; the unplayable file means the audio was truncated by the synchronous size limit; and the empty second read is a bug in the client library

checks.prompt: Model the request planner and the pricing. Define `ENGINES` mapping `"standard"` to 4.0 per million characters with 5000000 free, `"neural"` to 16.0 with 1000000 free, `"long-form"` to 100.0 with 500000 free and `"generative"` to 30.0 with 100000 free; and the limits `SYNC_TOTAL, SYNC_BILLED = 6000, 3000` and `ASYNC_TOTAL, ASYNC_BILLED = 200000, 100000`. Write `total_characters(text)` returning its length, and `billed_characters(text, text_type="text")` returning the length for plain text, the length with every `<…>` tag removed for markup, and raising `ValueError` for any other type. Write `monthly_cost(chars, engine)` charging only the amount beyond that engine's free allowance, raising `ValueError` for an unknown engine. Write `plan_request(text, voice, engine, voices, text_type="text")`, where `voices` maps a voice name to the engines it supports: raise `ValueError` for an unknown engine, an unknown voice, or a voice that does not support the engine; raise `ValueError` if the total exceeds `ASYNC_TOTAL` or the billed count exceeds `ASYNC_BILLED`; and otherwise return `{"api", "total", "billed", "cost"}`, where `api` is the synchronous call name when BOTH the total is within `SYNC_TOTAL` and the billed count within `SYNC_BILLED`, and the asynchronous task name otherwise. Write `wrap_pcm(raw, sample_rate=16000)` returning the bytes of a single-channel, two-byte-per-sample wave file containing those raw samples. Standard library only.
checks.explanation: The heavily marked-up document in the middle is the case worth remembering: four hundred billed characters — a tenth of the inline ceiling — and yet it cannot be sent inline, because the tags are free but they are still bytes on the request. Two counts, two different jobs: one decides the bill, the other decides which call you make. The engine assertions encode the other everyday trap, which is that engines belong to voices rather than to callers, so the pairing is something you look up rather than assume. The pricing block shows why that matters commercially — the ladder spans a factor of twenty-five, and the same monthly volume is free on the cheapest engine and hundreds of pounds on the priciest. And the last block is the quiet one: raw samples arrive with no header at all, so what makes them playable is a container you add, not anything the service did wrong.
checks.test:
import io
import wave

VOICES = {
    "Joanna": ("standard", "neural", "long-form", "generative"),
    "Matthew": ("standard", "neural"),
    "Ivy": ("standard",),
}

# Only the spoken words are billed; the markup is free.
plain = "Breaking news."
ssml = ("<speak><amazon:domain name='news'>Breaking news."
        "<break time='400ms'/></amazon:domain></speak>")
assert billed_characters(plain) == 14
assert billed_characters(ssml, "ssml") == 14, billed_characters(ssml, "ssml")
assert total_characters(ssml) == 93, total_characters(ssml)
assert total_characters(ssml) > 6 * billed_characters(ssml, "ssml")
try:
    billed_characters("x", "plaintext")
except ValueError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("an unknown text type must be refused")

# ...but the markup still counts toward the SIZE of the request, which is why a
# document can be far under the billed cap and still be too big to send inline.
heavy = "<speak>" + ("<emphasis level='strong'>ab</emphasis>" * 200) + "</speak>"
assert billed_characters(heavy, "ssml") == 400
assert total_characters(heavy) > 6_000
plan = plan_request(heavy, "Joanna", "neural", VOICES, text_type="ssml")
assert plan["api"] == "start_speech_synthesis_task", plan
assert plan["billed"] == 400 and plan["total"] > 6_000, plan

# Short text goes inline...
short = plan_request("Hello there.", "Joanna", "neural", VOICES)
assert short == {"api": "synthesize_speech", "total": 12, "billed": 12,
                 "cost": 0.0}, short
assert plan_request("x" * 6_000, "Joanna", "neural", VOICES)["api"] == \
    "start_speech_synthesis_task"
assert plan_request("x" * 3_000, "Joanna", "neural", VOICES)["api"] == \
    "synthesize_speech"
assert plan_request("x" * 3_001, "Joanna", "neural", VOICES)["api"] == \
    "start_speech_synthesis_task"

# ...and even the asynchronous route has a ceiling.
for oversize in ("x" * 100_001, "y" * 200_001):
    try:
        plan_request(oversize, "Joanna", "neural", VOICES)
    except ValueError:
        continue
    raise AssertionError("beyond the asynchronous limit must be refused")

# Engines are a property of the VOICE, not a free choice: the pairing is checked
# rather than assumed.
plan_request("hi", "Matthew", "neural", VOICES)
for bad in (("Matthew", "generative"), ("Ivy", "neural"), ("Nobody", "neural"),
            ("Joanna", "ultra")):
    try:
        plan_request("hi", bad[0], bad[1], VOICES)
    except ValueError:
        continue
    raise AssertionError(f"{bad} must be refused")

# The quality ladder is also a price ladder, and the gap is large.
assert monthly_cost(3_000_000, "standard") == 0.0
assert monthly_cost(3_000_000, "neural") == 32.0
assert monthly_cost(3_000_000, "generative") == 87.0
assert monthly_cost(3_000_000, "long-form") == 250.0
assert monthly_cost(3_000_000, "long-form") > 7 * monthly_cost(3_000_000, "neural")
assert monthly_cost(1_000_000, "neural") == 0.0
assert monthly_cost(0, "long-form") == 0.0
try:
    monthly_cost(10, "fancy")
except ValueError:
    pass
else:
    raise AssertionError("an unknown engine must be refused")

# Raw samples come back with NO container, so writing them straight to a file
# produces something nothing will play until a header is added.
raw = b"".join(int(0).to_bytes(2, "little", signed=True) for _ in range(100))
wrapped = wrap_pcm(raw, 16000)
assert wrapped[:4] == b"RIFF" and wrapped[8:12] == b"WAVE", wrapped[:12]
assert raw[:4] != b"RIFF"
assert len(wrapped) > len(raw)
with wave.open(io.BytesIO(wrapped), "rb") as reader:
    assert reader.getnchannels() == 1
    assert reader.getsampwidth() == 2
    assert reader.getframerate() == 16000
    assert reader.getnframes() == 100
    assert reader.readframes(100) == raw
# The samples themselves are untouched -- only a header was added.
assert wrapped.endswith(raw)
assert wave.open(io.BytesIO(wrap_pcm(raw, 24000)), "rb").getframerate() == 24000

checks.prompt: A team ships an article-narration feature that works in testing and fails in production on longer articles, with an exception about text length. They also find that a pronunciation fix they uploaded for their brand name has no effect, and that a voice available in the documentation is missing in their region. What is the correct assessment?
checks.explanation: Three deployment realities. The inline call has a hard character ceiling and anything longer must go through the asynchronous task that writes to object storage and is polled — that is an architectural decision, not a retry. Uploaded pronunciation lexicons are regional and opt-in: they apply only when named on the request. And the service is regional in its feature set as well as its endpoints, so newer engines and voices appear in some regions before others.
options: Long articles exceed the inline call's ceiling and must go through the asynchronous task that writes to object storage and is polled for completion — a design decision to make before shipping, not after. The pronunciation fix is a lexicon, which lives in one region and applies only when named on the request; uploading it does not make it automatic or global. And engines and voices roll out per region, so a voice present elsewhere may not exist in theirs, and cross-region calls add latency
Long articles simply need to be retried with a larger timeout; the lexicon takes effect after a propagation delay; and the missing voice indicates an out-of-date client library
The length exception means markup was billed and pushed them over; removing the markup resolves it, and the lexicon and voice problems are both permission issues
Long articles require the most expressive engine, which raises the limit; the lexicon must be embedded in the markup rather than uploaded; and voices are global, so the missing one is a naming error

checks.prompt: Compare this service with the equivalent offerings from the other two major clouds, with the specialist naturalness leader, and with a self-hosted open engine. Say what each wins on and what it costs. Then advise a company on this cloud publishing 200 long-form articles a month as audio, needing synchronised text highlighting in their reader, and wanting a recognisable house voice. Say what you would use and what you would tell them about the last requirement.
checks.expected: A correct answer must position all four. This service wins on being native to its cloud — identity, regional endpoints, object storage for asynchronous output — with an engine ladder including a long-form tier, timing metadata for captions and lip-sync, and per-character billing where markup is free; the costs are that it is cloud-only, synthesis only with recognition being a separate service, that its top expressive quality trails the specialist, and that there is no instant voice cloning. The other clouds' services are comparable in quality and the right answer when native to those platforms; one of them notably bills markup characters and offers a unified toolkit spanning recognition and synthesis, which is a genuine difference. The specialist wins on naturalness and instant cloning, at the cost of price at the quality tier and much weaker enterprise identity plumbing. A self-hosted open engine wins on running offline with no per-use bill, at the cost of running the infrastructure and quality that trails. The recommendation must be this service, justified by the concrete requirements: they are already on the cloud, the long-form engine exists for exactly this content, timing metadata gives the reader's highlighting directly rather than requiring separate alignment, and long articles route naturally through the asynchronous task into object storage. The cost caveat must be raised — the long-form tier is by far the priciest per character, so 200 articles a month deserves an explicit estimate and a comparison against the neural tier. The house voice must be handled honestly: there is no instant cloning here; a custom brand voice exists only as a gated custom engagement, so the practical options are choosing a distinctive catalogue voice and using it consistently, or going to the specialist vendor for a cloned voice and accepting a second supplier. Noting that a pronunciation lexicon is the right tool for making the brand name always come out correctly is a plus.
